title: Why You Must Never Confuse Fun And Hard Work https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/09/26/why-you-must-never-confuse-fun-and-hard-work/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin affirms his belief in bringing genuine fun, humor, and dynamic teaching into the classroom, but warns against a growing danger: treating fun as the goal itself rather than as a tool that opens the door to serious academic work. He argues that constantly trying to make every lesson entertaining sends students the harmful message that only fun activities have value, compounding a cultural trend already driven by screens and short-form media that shortens attention spans. His prescription is a two-part teaching model: bring energy, humor, and dramatization to open the door to learning, then step back and require sustained, effortful, independent engagement — reading, writing, discussing, struggling — that builds grit and deep thinking. He rejects the idea that students have a fixed capacity for attentiveness, insisting instead that stamina for hard work can and must be deliberately built. The reward for this balance, he writes, is a productive, engaged class that is genuinely transformed by the end of the year.
points: Fun and humor are valuable tools that open the door to learning, but they must not be mistaken for learning itself.
Treating every lesson as entertainment teaches students that only fun activities have worth, undermining academic rigor.
Modern distractions like social media and short-form video are already shortening student attention spans, requiring deliberate counterbalancing.
Students' capacity for sustained attention and hard work is not fixed — it can and must be built through practice.
Balancing engaging instruction with demanding independent work produces a genuinely transformed, productive class over time.
quotes: Fun is merely a tool. Although real and wonderful, it’s a tool that opens the door to learning. It isn’t learning itself—at least, it shouldn’t be most of the time.
You see, the danger in trying to make every lesson an inflatable bounce house is that you send the message that if it isn’t fun, then it doesn’t have value and therefore isn’t worth doing.
With excessive television, video games, text messaging, social media, and the like conspiring to shorten attention spans and weaken observational power, we must provide the counterpoint.
Your job is to provide world-class instruction, to emote, mimic, and dramatize, to bring the curriculum to life for your students . . . and then turn responsibility over to them.
Although our students come to us with varying levels of attentiveness, they can all improve. The idea that they have a fixed ability of which we can do little about is hogwash.
But the rewards are no less than a productive, well-behaved class who can’t wait to get to school every day.
